about: Single-pole miniature circuit breaker for one final circuit, protecting against overload and short circuit. Pick the curve for the load: B for resistive and lighting, C for general mixed loads, D for high-inrush motors and transformers.
Two-pole MCB that breaks line and neutral together, common on single-phase circuits where full isolation is required for maintenance.
Three-pole MCB for three-phase loads. All three poles trip together so a fault on one phase cannot leave a motor running single-phased.
Four-pole MCB breaking three phases plus neutral, used where the neutral must be isolated, such as on generator or changeover circuits.
One pole plus switched neutral in a single module width, the usual choice for apartment and lighting boards where DIN space is tight.
Industrial-grade MCB with a higher breaking capacity than domestic ranges. Specify where the prospective short-circuit current at the board exceeds what a standard 6kA device can clear.
MCB built to UL and CSA ratings for panels destined for North American markets or for machinery exported there.
Standard Acti9 MCB at 6kA breaking capacity, suitable for most commercial final circuits. Pairs with Vigi add-on blocks if earth-leakage protection is needed later.
Higher breaking capacity version of the iC60 for boards closer to the transformer where fault levels are greater.
General purpose SENTRON MCB for final circuit protection across lighting, socket and small power circuits.
Compact economy MCB for high-volume repeat circuits in residential and light commercial boards.
Eaton MCB range with a wide curve and rating selection, frequently specified in machine-building and OEM panels.
Combined MCB and residual current device in one module: overload, short-circuit and earth-leakage protection for a single circuit. Common at 30mA for socket outlets requiring additional protection.
Two-pole RCBO providing overcurrent and earth-leakage protection while isolating both line and neutral.
Three-pole RCBO for three-phase circuits needing residual current protection without a separate upstream RCCB.
Four-pole RCBO covering three phases and neutral. Used where individual circuit discrimination matters more than a single shared RCCB.
Higher breaking capacity RCBO range for boards with elevated fault levels where a standard 6kA device would be inadequate.
Acti9 RCBO in one module width, giving each circuit its own earth-leakage protection so a single fault does not trip an entire board section.

Residual current circuit breaker detecting earth leakage but offering no overload protection, so it always sits behind or above separate overcurrent devices. Choose the type by load: AC for simple resistive, A where electronics are present, B where drives or DC components can produce smooth residual currents.

Residual current circuit breaker protecting a group of circuits against earth leakage. At 30mA it provides additional protection against electric shock; at 300mA it is normally used for fire protection on a whole section.
Acti9 residual current device available in Type A and Type B. Type B is required where variable speed drives can produce smooth DC residual current that would blind a Type AC device.
SENTRON RCCB for group earth-leakage protection. Consider splitting circuits across several RCCBs so one nuisance trip does not take out an entire board.
160A moulded case breaker for outgoing ways on small distribution boards. Classes set interrupting capacity only: B 18, C 25, N 36, S 50, H 70 kA at 415V.
160A frame taking thermal-magnetic or Ekip trip units for selectivity against downstream devices. Classes: N 36, S 50, H 70, L 120, V 150 kA at 415V.
250A frame for mid-size feeders and sub-board supplies, normally with a TMA trip unit. Classes: C 25, N 36, S 50 kA at 415V.
250A frame with electronic trip options where settings must coordinate with upstream protection. Classes: N 36, S 50, H 70, L 120, V 150, X 200 kA at 415V.
630A frame for major feeders and transformer outgoings, usually 400A or 630A. Classes: N 36, S 50, H 70, L 120, V 150, X 200 kA at 415V.
1000A frame for main incomers and large plant, usually 630A, 800A or 1000A. Classes: N 36, S 50, H 70 kA at 415V.
1600A frame for main incoming protection where an air circuit breaker is not needed, usually 800A to 1600A. Classes: S 50, H 70, L 120 kA at 415V.
XT7 with a stored-energy mechanism for rapid or remote closing. The M is the mechanism, not a trip unit. Classes: S 50, H 70, L 120 kA at 415V.
Compact NSX moulded case breaker with interchangeable TM or Micrologic trip units. The electronic units add metering and adjustable protection curves.
Cost-focused moulded case breaker for standard distribution feeders where adjustable electronic protection is not required.
SENTRON moulded case breaker with thermal-magnetic trip for general distribution feeders.
SENTRON breaker with electronic trip units and optional communications, suited to boards where energy data and selectivity are both required.
Eaton moulded case breaker range covering a wide band of frame sizes, common as both incomer and outgoing protection in industrial boards.
Compact moulded case breaker for smaller feeders where space in the board is limited.

Air circuit breaker for main incoming protection at high current, typically above 800A. Decide early whether it is fixed or withdrawable, since withdrawable versions need far more depth and a defined racking area in front of the board.
The SACE Emax 2 range, in the E1.2, E2.2, E4.2 and E6.2 frames. Fixed or withdrawable, with Ekip trip units covering protection, metering and communications.
Main air circuit breaker with Micrologic X control units providing measurement, diagnostics and remote connectivity. Common as the incomer on large main LV boards.
SENTRON air circuit breaker for main and coupler positions. Confirm the trip unit family early since it drives the metering and communications you can offer later.
Compact air circuit breaker for main protection where panel depth is constrained but ACB features are still required.
1600A air circuit breaker frame. Classes B, C, N and L set short-circuit performance, not a trip curve. Icu depends on class and voltage; take it from the ABB table.
2500A frame with classes B, N, S and H. The letter is a short-circuit performance level only; an E2.2N is not an N trip curve.
4000A frame with classes N, S, H and V, high-performance versions reaching about 150kA. Do not apply the family maximum to every breaker.
6300A frame with classes H, V and X. Never carry a Tmax XT breaking-capacity figure across to an Emax 2: the letters do not mean the same kA.
Legacy ABB Emax families. They do not map onto E1.2-E6.2, so check spare-parts compatibility and any retrofit kit before treating one as a replacement.

Surge protection device diverting transient overvoltage from lightning and switching to earth. Type 1 goes at the origin where there is a lightning protection system, Type 2 at distribution boards. It needs a correctly rated backup fuse or breaker and the shortest possible connecting leads.
Type 2 SPD for induced lightning and switching surges in distribution boards. Selected on In and Imax, not on kA alone. P is pluggable, TS adds remote signalling.
Acti9 surge protection with a status window showing when the cartridge is spent, and a remote signalling contact so a failed arrester does not sit unnoticed.
Pluggable surge protection where the protection module can be replaced without disturbing the wiring, useful on boards in high-exposure locations.

Arc fault detection device recognising the signature of a series or parallel arcing fault that a normal MCB or RCD will not see. Specified for fire risk areas such as sleeping accommodation and timber structures.
Arc fault detection combined with overcurrent protection in one device, reducing the DIN width needed compared with separate units.
Residual current monitor that measures and reports leakage continuously instead of tripping, letting you catch a deteriorating circuit before it causes an outage.
Type 1 SPD for partial or direct lightning current at the service entrance. Selected on Iimp. A low Up is not implied, so a Type 2 stage often follows it.
Combined Type 1+2 for main distribution, covering lightning current and switching surges in one device. OVR T1-T2-T3 adds a Type 3 stage for a lower protection level.
Combined Type 2+3 for final distribution and sensitive equipment, where a Type 2 stage alone leaves the protection level too high.
Type 3 SPD installed near sensitive equipment, the lowest-energy stage. It must sit downstream of a Type 1 or Type 2 and is not a service-entrance device.
SPD for PV strings, combiners and inverter DC inputs. Rated on maximum continuous DC voltage. An AC SPD must never be fitted to a DC PV circuit.
SPD for telephone, signal and communication lines. Selected on signal voltage, bandwidth and insertion loss, not on a mains rating.
North American OVR ranges for control panels, residential service entrances and commercial panels. Rated to UL with MCOV, VPR and SCCR: keep apart from the IEC rows.
Load break switch providing a visible, lockable point of isolation so a board or section can be worked on safely. Rated for making and breaking load current, unlike a plain disconnector.
Switch disconnector for main isolation or outgoing feeders, available with door-coupled rotary handles that can be padlocked off for safe working.
Load break switch for isolation duty on incomers and outgoing feeders where switching capability without protection is required.
Switch-disconnector in the XT1 frame, to 160A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT2 frame, to 160A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT3 frame, to 250A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT4 frame, to 250A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT5 frame, to 630A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT6 frame, to 1000A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT7 frame, to 1600A. No trip unit: it will not clear a fault and needs protection upstream.
Switch-disconnector in the XT7 frame with a stored-energy mechanism. No trip unit: it needs protection upstream.
Manual changeover switch selecting between two supplies, typically utility and generator. The I-0-II arrangement mechanically prevents both sources being connected at once.
Motorised changeover switch for automatic transfer between utility and generator, mechanically interlocked so both sources can never be paralleled.

Automatic transfer controller monitoring the normal supply and commanding changeover to the standby source. Set the transfer and return delays deliberately so brief dips do not start the generator unnecessarily.

Auto mains failure controller starting the generator on supply loss, transferring load and returning it once the mains is stable. It needs clear wiring to the generator start contacts and both source sensing points.
Emax 2 switch-disconnector in the E1.2 frame. MS is neither a motor starter nor a magnetic trip: there is no trip unit and it needs protection upstream.
Emax 2 switch-disconnector in the E2.2 frame. No trip unit, so it provides isolation only and depends on an upstream protective device.
Emax 2 switch-disconnector in the E4.2 frame. No trip unit, so it provides isolation only and depends on an upstream protective device.
Emax 2 switch-disconnector in the E6.2 frame. No trip unit, so it provides isolation only and depends on an upstream protective device.

NH fuse link giving very high breaking capacity in a compact body, often used ahead of large feeders or where the fault level exceeds what a breaker can handle economically. gG is for general cable protection, aM for motor circuits.
DIN rail fuse carrier holding cartridge or NH fuse links, giving isolation when the carrier is withdrawn. Confirm the fuse size it accepts and whether a blown-fuse indicator is required.
Cylindrical fuse links in 8.5x31.5, 10x38, 14x51 and 22x58mm. Class decides the duty: gG is full range, aM is short circuit only and needs a separate overload relay.
DIN-rail fuse holder and disconnector for cylindrical links, E91 to E94 by pole count. The holder class is its maximum, not the fitted fuse: an E93/32 may hold 16A links.
PV fuse disconnector for photovoltaic strings, the PV1500 version rated to 1500V DC. Do not fit an AC-rated holder or link to a PV circuit.
Knife-blade HRC fuse links for distribution and industrial protection, high breaking capacity and strongly current limiting. Current does not follow from NH size alone.
Fixed base for NH fuse links, open or IP20 protected. A base protects nothing on its own: protection comes from the link fitted to it.
Switch fuse combining load switching, isolation and fuse protection in one device. Record frame current, fuse size and the current of the link actually fitted.
Motor-operated switch fuse for remote or automatic operation in transfer and process schemes. Motor control voltage is separate from the power-circuit voltage.
Compact fuse-switch disconnector for distribution boards, taking NH links according to frame. Optional fuse monitoring.
Busbar-mounted fuse-switch disconnector in a vertical arrangement, for cable distribution and industrial boards. Electronic fuse monitoring available.
Switch-disconnector-fuse for distribution and industrial switchboards, compact on busbar installations.
High-performance fusegear for PV and elevated-voltage applications. Verify the exact AC or DC rating against the product record before applying it.
Outdoor utility cable-distribution system with fuse-switch and busbar components. Not a DIN-rail product and not interchangeable with one.
Electronic fuse monitoring and intelligent monitoring units reporting per-phase fuse state, current and temperature. A striker fuse alone gives no remote signal.
Three-pole AF contactor, 18A AC-3 at 400V, about 7.5kW, for small motors and controlled loads. In AF16-30-10-13 the blocks are frame, main poles, auxiliaries, coil.
Mid-size three-pole AF at 26A AC-3 at 400V, about 11kW, with no built-in auxiliary. Add-on blocks mount front or side.
Three-pole AF at 38A AC-3 at 400V, about 18.5kW. Size on the AC-3 figure against motor full-load amps; the AC-1 rating of the same frame is higher.
The main ABB motor contactor range, AF09 to AF2850, roughly 4kW to 560kW at 400V AC-3. The number after AF is a frame size, not a current: AF16 is 18A AC-3, not 16A.
Low-consumption AF for PLC control and supplies prone to voltage dips. Coil code 30 is a dedicated 24V DC PLC coil. Not interchangeable with standard AF.
AF built for safety-related switching, with mirror and mechanically linked contacts. The contactor alone does not set a performance level. Never substitute a plain AF.
AC-control contactor family. Preserve the coil-voltage suffix: the standard AF wide-band AC/DC coil data does not apply.
Railway-qualified AF for rolling stock, built for vibration, shock and fire and smoke requirements. RT is the ring-tongue terminal version.
Compact AC-operated mini-contactor to about 5.5kW at 400V AC-3. Screw, solder-pin and flat-pin terminals.
DC-operated mini-contactor for compact motor and power switching. The DC coil is what separates it from the B family.
Higher-performance mini-contactor with AC or DC coil options and several terminal types.
Capacitor contactor for power-factor correction banks, rated in AC-6b kvar rather than motor amps. The RA version adds damping resistors.
DC-switching contactor for PV, battery storage, EV charging and DC distribution. An AC current rating never transfers to DC duty.
Modular DIN-rail installation contactor, about 16 to 100A, for lighting, heating, ventilation and pumps. Hum-free AC/DC design.
Installation contactor with a manual and automatic selector, for building loads that need an override at the board.
Definite-purpose contactor for HVAC, refrigeration and compressors, about 20 to 75A. Rated to UL/CSA, not the IEC AF structure.
North American motor contactor sized by NEMA size rather than an IEC frame. Rated to UL/CSA.
Lighting contactor for commercial and industrial lighting. Lamp loads switch under AC-5a or AC-5b, not a motor AC-3 rating.
Legacy conventional-coil contactor in older installations. An AF is the usual replacement, but coil and accessories do not map across one for one.
Legacy DC-coil contactor from older DC-controlled installations.
Legacy ABB contactor family. Keep the exact type number and check the ABB cross-reference before assuming an AF equivalent.
Legacy large contactor from older high-current installations. Replacement contact sets and coils are ZL and ZAF items.
Four-pole AF for non-inductive loads, neutral switching and distribution. Not a substitute for a three-pole AF on motor duty.
AX three-pole contactors to 690V, frames AX09 to AX260. Not in the current ABB family classification, so verify before relying on it.
Capacitor contactor with damping resistors, which cut the inrush peak as a stage energises. Rated in AC-6b kvar; a motor contactor welds on this duty.
Large DC-switching contactor for high-current DC. A DC arc has no current zero to extinguish at, so an AC contactor is not a substitute.
TeSys D contactor, the workhorse for motor starters and load switching. Add-on auxiliary blocks and mechanical interlocks let it build reversing and star-delta arrangements.
SIRIUS contactor sized by frame across a wide kW range, designed to clip together with matching 3RU or 3RB overload relays into a compact starter.
Eaton DILM contactor range with matching overloads and accessory blocks, common in machine control panels.
Machinery drive for conveyors, mixers and small pumps, built for panel mounting with straightforward parameter setup.
General purpose drive covering most building services and industrial motor loads, with a built-in choke that reduces harmonic current without an external reactor.
HVAC variant tuned for fans and pumps, including firefighter override and PID control for pressure and flow.
Industrial drive for demanding applications including regenerative and common DC bus configurations. Confirm cooling and cabinet depth early, since larger frames are substantial.
Entry-level drive for small machines and single-phase supplies, typically fitted straight onto the machine panel.
Compact machine drive available in book and compact formats, with integrated safety functions such as Safe Torque Off.
High performance drive for dynamic machine control where fast response and precise speed regulation matter.
Process drive for pumps, fans and compressors with energy-saving control and built-in EMC filtering.
Basic drive for simple fan, pump and conveyor duties where a full parameter set would be overkill.
Compact single-unit drive combining control and power in one housing, saving panel width against the modular G120.
Modular drive where control unit and power module are selected separately, so the same power module can serve different control and communication needs.
Micro drive for basic speed control on small motors, common in HVAC and simple machinery.
Drive tuned for water and wastewater duty, with pump-specific features such as dry-run detection, pipe fill and cascade control.
Automation drive for demanding motor control including closed loop and servo-like applications.
Compact vector drive giving good torque control in a small footprint, widely used in OEM machine panels.
Heavy duty vector drive for cranes, hoists and high-torque applications where overload capability matters.
Compact drive for basic speed control, sized for small panels and simple commissioning.
General purpose drive with active energy control, used across pump, fan and conveyor duties.

Ramps motor voltage up and down to limit inrush current and mechanical shock on belts, couplings and pumps. Confirm whether a bypass is built in, and remember it still needs upstream isolation and overload protection.
Compact soft starter for small motors where the aim is simply to take the shock out of starting. No internal bypass, so allow for the heat it dissipates while ramping.
Soft starter with internal bypass and current limiting, so it stops dissipating heat once the motor is up to speed.
Advanced soft starter with built-in bypass, torque control and motor protection, suitable for large pumps and compressors where starting stress is a real problem.
Basic soft starter for small motors, providing a simple voltage ramp without configurable protection.
Soft starter with torque control giving smoother starts and stops on pumps, which reduces water hammer in pipework.
Advanced soft starter with integrated bypass, protection and diagnostics for larger motors and critical duties.
Standard soft starter for straightforward ramp starting on general purpose motors.
Soft starter combining bypass and motor protection in one device, reducing the component count in the starter section.
High-feature soft starter for large motors with adjustable torque control and comprehensive protection and diagnostics.
Soft starter with integrated bypass controlling two phases, compact enough to fit where a full three-phase controlled unit would not.
Standard manual motor starter, thermal and magnetic protection. The suffix is the top of an adjustable range, not a fixed trip: MS116-16 adjusts 10-16A.
Higher-performance manual motor starter with separate trip and magnetic-trip indication and a lockable handle. Icu varies by suffix and voltage.
MS132 protection with push-in spring terminals for tool-free wiring and no retightening. Stock separately from the screw-terminal MS132.
Higher-current manual motor starter, 10 to 80A. Trip indication and lockable handle. Short-circuit capacity depends on the rating and voltage.
Short-circuit protection only, with no thermal overload release. A motor needs a separate overload relay: this does not protect one on its own.
Magnetic-only protector to the 80A class. No thermal overload release, so a separate overload relay is required for motor duty.
Transformer version with a trip characteristic that tolerates energisation inrush. Select on transformer rating, not motor full-load current. KT is the push-in variant.
Lamp-circuit version for loads with lamp-starting inrush. Not an ordinary motor protector: select on lamp type, wattage and starting current.
Older ABB motor-protection families including MS225, MS325, MO325, MS450 and MS495. Accessories often do not fit current MS1xx devices.
TeSys manual motor starter with thermal-magnetic protection and a rotary handle, commonly the first device in a compact motor feeder.
Larger TeSys motor circuit breaker for mid-size motors, often paired with a matching contactor to form a compact starter.
SIRIUS motor starter protector that clips directly to matching 3RT contactors, forming a tested combination without extra wiring.
Motor protective circuit breaker with adjustable overload, used as a compact combined isolator and protection device.
Thermal overload relay protecting a motor from sustained overcurrent such as a jammed load or lost phase. Set the dial to motor full-load amps and check the trip class suits the starting time.

Thermal overload relay mounting directly onto matching contactors. Set the dial to motor full-load amps, and reset behaviour should be chosen deliberately since automatic reset on a motor can restart machinery.
Electronic overload relay with a wider setting range and selectable trip class, holding accuracy better than a bimetallic relay across ambient changes.
TeSys thermal overload relay clipping onto LC1D contactors, the standard partner in a Schneider motor starter.
Electronic overload relay for larger motors, with a wide adjustment range and better protection against phase loss.
Thermal overload relay designed to mount directly on 3RT contactors, forming a compact tested starter combination.
Electronic overload relay with selectable trip class from 5 to 30, useful for motors with long run-up times such as large fans.

Direct-on-line starter combining contactor and overload for the simplest motor start. Draws six to eight times full-load current at start, so confirm the supply and any generator can accept that step.

Star-delta starter reducing starting current by first running the motor in star, then switching to delta. The motor must have all six leads available and the transition timer needs setting to the actual run-up time.

Reversing starter using two mechanically and electrically interlocked contactors to swap two phases. The interlock is a safety requirement, not an option, since both closing together is a direct phase-to-phase fault.

Control transformer stepping the panel supply down to a separate control voltage, typically 230V or 110V, and isolating the control circuit from the power circuit. Size the VA for the inrush of all contactor coils picking up together, not just their holding current.
Basic 24VDC supply for small control loads such as a handful of relays and sensors, where power reserve features are unnecessary.
Mid-range 24VDC supply for typical control panels, with a stable output and compact DIN footprint.
Premium 24VDC supply whose selective fuse breaking technology delivers extra current briefly, so a downstream fault clears its protective device instead of dragging the whole 24V rail down.
Compact 24VDC supply for small control tasks where DIN width is at a premium.
General purpose 24VDC supply covering most panel control loads, with adjustable output voltage to compensate for line drop.
Single-phase SITOP supply for control circuits and SIMATIC controllers, with reserve capacity for short overloads.
Three-phase SITOP supply for larger 24VDC loads, balancing the draw across all three phases rather than loading one.
Economical DIN rail supply for light control duties, widely used in OEM panels.
Ultra-slim DIN supply for tight enclosures where every millimetre of rail counts.
Higher power DIN supply for panels with substantial 24VDC load such as banks of valves or extensive I/O.
Three-phase DIN supply for heavy 24VDC loads, keeping phase loading balanced on larger installations.
CliQ series supply available in single and three-phase versions with good efficiency and a compact footprint.
General purpose 24VDC supply for control circuits, with models sized from small interface duty upward.
DC uninterruptible supply with intelligent battery management that reports remaining backup time, so control power outlives a brief mains loss.
Managed DC-UPS with configurable buffer time and diagnostics over the controller network, letting a PLC shut down cleanly rather than dying mid-operation.
Redundancy and buffer module decoupling two power supplies so a single failed unit cannot pull down the shared 24V rail.
DIN rail supply with an integrated battery charger and changeover, a cost-effective route to backed-up control power on smaller panels.

Programmable logic controller running the panel control sequence. Count the digital and analogue I/O needed with spare capacity, and confirm the communication protocol before fixing the enclosure layout.
Compact controller for panel automation with expandable digital and analogue I/O. Confirm the I/O count with spare capacity and whether PROFINET or Modbus is required before finalising the layout.
Machine controller for pump, HVAC and small process panels, with built-in Ethernet on most references.
Modular controller that scales from small to large I/O counts, useful where the same panel design must cover several plant sizes.
Cost-effective compact PLC widely used in OEM machine panels with straightforward digital and analogue expansion.
Door-mounted touch panel giving the operator status, alarms and setpoints. Cutting the door aperture accurately matters, and the IP rating only holds if the supplied gasket is fitted correctly.
Compact operator terminal for smaller panels where a full PC-based interface is unnecessary.
Time relay providing on-delay, off-delay or cyclic switching for sequencing, pump alternation and star-delta transitions.
Multifunction timer covering on-delay, off-delay, interval and cyclic modes in one part, which cuts down on stocked variants.

Safety relay monitoring emergency stops, guard switches and light curtains, providing a redundant and monitored trip path. It must be wired to the documented category and cannot be bypassed by ordinary control logic.
Safety relay for emergency stop and guard monitoring with expandable output modules for larger safety circuits.
Contactor relay for control circuits. No main power poles, which is what separates it from a four-pole contactor. Arrangements from 2NO+2NC up to 8NO.
Low-consumption contactor relay for PLC and control circuits, the NF equivalent of AFZ.
AC-control contactor relay. Preserve the coil-voltage suffix; NF wide-band coil data does not apply.
Railway-qualified contactor relay for rolling-stock control circuits. RT is the ring-tongue terminal version.
Four-pole mini contactor relay for compact control circuits. A relay, not a mini power contactor.
Interface relay isolating low-power controller outputs from the coils and loads they switch, and converting between control voltages. The slim DIN format keeps a dense I/O interface tidy.
Slim plug-in interface relay isolating controller outputs from field loads. The pluggable design lets a failed relay be swapped without disturbing terminal wiring.
General purpose plug-in relay with a socket base, used for interposing and simple control logic in panels of every size.
Three-phase monitoring relay detecting phase loss, wrong phase sequence, under and overvoltage. It is what stops a motor running single-phased after an upstream fuse clears one leg.
Line monitoring relay for phase sequence, asymmetry and voltage window, commonly interlocked into the start circuit of motor panels.
Panel-mounted digital meter showing voltage, current and basic energy values on the board door. Confirm whether it measures directly or needs current transformers.
DIN rail energy meter for sub-billing and consumption monitoring, available in direct-connect and CT versions with Modbus output.
Door-mounted multifunction meter showing the full set of electrical values with Modbus or PROFINET reporting.
Compact DIN rail energy meter widely used for sub-metering individual feeders in tenant and process installations.
Power quality analyser recording harmonics, power factor, demand and event data, usually reporting over Modbus to a monitoring system. Specify where energy billing or harmonic problems need evidence.
Panel-mounted power meter measuring energy, demand and basic power quality, suited to tenant metering and energy management.
Advanced meter adding harmonic analysis and data logging, used where power quality has to be proven rather than assumed.
Network analyser recording power quality and harmonic content, typically fitted where drives and non-linear loads dominate.

Current transformer scaling feeder current down to a meter input, usually 5A or 1A. Match the ratio and accuracy class to the meter, and never leave the secondary open circuit while primary current flows.
Test block allowing meters and protection relays to be tested or replaced without breaking the CT secondary, which it shorts automatically as the plug is withdrawn.
Power factor controller switching capacitor stages to hold the target power factor and avoid reactive energy charges. Set the target and the C/k ratio to suit the CT and the smallest stage.
Power factor controller with stage health monitoring, which matters because a failed capacitor stage otherwise goes unnoticed until the bill rises.
Dry-type power capacitor forming the stages of a correction bank. Capacitors need discharge resistors and adequate ventilation, and they age faster in hot or harmonic-rich environments.
Detuned reactor placed in series with capacitor stages to shift the resonant frequency away from prevailing harmonics. Required wherever significant drive or UPS load shares the installation.
Line or load reactor fitted with a drive to reduce current distortion, protect the drive input and limit voltage stress on long motor cables.
Active filter injecting counter-current to cancel harmonics in real time. Specify from a measured harmonic survey rather than assumption, since sizing depends on the actual spectrum.
Screw-clamp terminal block for field wiring connections. Grouping terminals by function and numbering them consistently is what makes later fault finding fast.
Screw clamp terminal range covering signal through power cross-sections in a consistent form, with matching bridges, markers and test accessories.
Push-in spring terminal that accepts a ferruled conductor without a tool, cutting wiring time and removing the retorquing that screw terminals need.
Spring clamp terminal that holds tension regardless of vibration or thermal cycling, which is why it is common on machinery and transport panels.
Push-in terminal system with a uniform accessory set across cross-sections, keeping cross-bridging and marking consistent through the panel.
Potential distribution block splitting one supply into many outgoing points, tidying up the 24VDC and earth distribution that otherwise turns into daisy-chained terminals.
Insulated distribution block taking one large incoming cable and splitting it to several outgoing ways without a full busbar system.
Bootlace ferrule terminating a stranded conductor so no strand escapes the terminal. Use the correct crimp tool and die, since an under-crimped ferrule becomes a hot joint.
Compression lug terminating large cables onto busbars and breaker pads. Match lug, die and tool from the same system, and confirm bolt torque against the manufacturer figure.
Printed markers identifying conductors and terminals to the drawing. Consistent numbering is the single thing that most reduces fault-finding time years later.
Slotted wiring duct routing and containing panel wiring. Leave real spare capacity, since ducts filled to the brim make later modifications painful and trap heat.
Cable gland sealing a cable where it enters the enclosure, maintaining the IP rating and providing strain relief. Metal glands additionally terminate cable armour or screen.
Standard 35mm DIN rail carrying modular devices. Plan rail heights and spacing around wiring duct so devices remain accessible after wiring.
Copper busbar system rated around 250A for distributing current across a board section, keeping outgoing connections short and consistent.
Higher rated busbar for main distribution sections, where cable connections to every outgoing device would be impractical.
Busbar system with component adaptors that clip devices directly onto the bars, cutting internal cabling and giving a repeatable, tested arrangement.
Copper bar carrying current between sections and devices inside the board. Size it for continuous current and short-circuit withstand, and check the support spacing for the fault level.
Flexible laminated connector between busbar and device, absorbing vibration and thermal movement and easing awkward connection geometry.
Insulated busbar support holding bars at a fixed spacing. Support spacing is a short-circuit withstand question, not a tidiness one: bars must not deflect together under fault forces.
Protective earth bar giving every circuit a common bonding point. It must be sized for the largest fault current and clearly labelled and accessible.
Neutral bar collecting circuit neutrals. Keep neutrals grouped with their own circuits so that RCD protection and later fault finding both work predictably.
Flexible bonding braid earthing doors and hinged plates. Doors carrying any electrical device must be bonded, and paint has to be removed at the fixing point for the bond to be real.
Compact wall-mounting enclosure for smaller boards and control panels. Confirm the IP rating survives every cut-out and gland you add to it.
Bayable floor-standing frame system for large boards, allowing sections to be joined into a lineup with continuous busbar and shared cable zones.

Filter fan drawing cooler outside air through the enclosure to remove heat from drives, transformers and breakers. It needs a matching exit filter, and the filter mats need a cleaning interval in the maintenance plan.
Filter fan with matched exit filter for forced ventilation. Size airflow from the calculated heat load and remember it can only cool to ambient, never below it.

Active cooling unit refrigerating the enclosure below ambient, needed where drives and transformers exceed what filtered ventilation can remove. It needs condensate management and a sealed enclosure to work correctly.
Panel heater preventing condensation in cold or outdoor enclosures. Condensation, not cold, is what damages electronics, so pair it with a hygrostat or thermostat.
Panel thermostat switching a fan or heater at a set temperature. Use a normally-closed unit for heating and a normally-open unit for cooling.
Hygrostat switching a heater on humidity rather than temperature, which is the more reliable way to keep an outdoor enclosure dry.
Interior LED light, usually with a door switch, so maintenance inside a deep board does not depend on a hand torch.
Service socket inside the enclosure for test equipment and tools. It should be fed from its own protected circuit with RCD protection.
Mechanical door interlock preventing the enclosure being opened while the main switch is closed, with a defeat facility for authorised testing.
Latching emergency stop with positively-driven normally-closed contacts. It must break the control path directly, not merely request a stop from a controller.
22mm door-mounted push button for start, stop and reset commands. Contact blocks are ordered separately, so confirm how many NO and NC contacts each function needs.
Metal-bezel control station range for doors, with a wide selection of heads and contact blocks that share one mounting cut-out.
Modular door control range with plastic and metal versions, and connection options from screw terminals to an integrated bus module.
Panel door selector switch giving a positive two or three position choice such as hand-off-auto. Confirm the contact arrangement matches the control logic before drilling the door.
Pilot light showing run, trip or supply-healthy status on the door. LED versions draw far less current and last longer than filament equivalents.
Analogue ammeter giving an at-a-glance load indication on the door. Still favoured on motor panels because a swinging needle shows a struggling load better than a digital readout.
Ammeter selector letting one meter read each phase in turn. It must be the CT-shorting type so the transformer secondary is never opened while switching.
